items.title: The DSA’s Problem Isn’t ‘Media Training’
items.description: American socialists are convinced that they have a media-training problem. In the past year, members of the Democratic Socialists of America, the country’s largest leftist organization, have won electoral victories in places such as New York City and Michigan, drawing a spotlight that the group has struggled to handle. Last month, the DSA’s co-chairs, Megan Romer and Ashik Siddique, gave several high-profile interviews that even many of their most fervent supporters agree were disastrous. The two leaders struggled to give straight answers to simple questions, and they defended outlandish policies, such as abolishing prisons and police. They seemed to present socialists exactly the way their opponents caricature them: as extremist, unserious, and unprepared. In damage-control mode, many of DSA’s defenders on social media are repeating the phrase media training as though it were a mantra . If only the group’s leaders had been better prepared to deal with media outlets , the thinking goes, they would have avoided this train wreck . The DSA’s communications director, Priscilla Yeverino, recently told Axios , “Our leaders aren’t politicians. They’re working-class people and new to doing media.” The idea that the DSA’s troubles on prime-time television are a technical matter solvable by the right training is surely comforting, but it is also wrong. The group has a bigger problem: It is led by unpractical extremists whose views are a far cry from those that its electorally successful figures, such as Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, espouse. [ Read: Why do rich kids love socialism? ] This disconnect is partly explained by a sharp division within the DSA. One wing engages in mass politics and includes AOC, Mamdani, and other socialists committed to democratic principles. The other wing is sectarian and extremist: It evinces little commitment to democracy and includes open admirers of Hamas, the Iranian regime, and historical dictators such as Mao Zedong. If the interviews with the DSA’s co-chairs were embarrassing, that’s a result not of a lackluster media performance but of the actual positions the group has embraced. A closer look at the interviews confirms this. Romer, who belongs to the sectarian wing, evidently did not know what the 2000 Camp David Summit was and could not say what “taxing the hell out of millionaires,” as she demanded, would look like in practice. When asked about authoritarianism in Cuba, she praised the country’s constitution and suggested that Americans should learn from it. Maybe media training could have taught Romer what happened at Camp David and what a tax policy might entail. It still wouldn’t have made the pro-authoritarian politics she shares with her faction of the DSA more palatable. In December, Romer’s Red Star caucus, a self-declared Marxist-Leninist faction of the DSA, posted quotes from a speech by Mao in “celebration” of the Chinese Communist leader’s 132nd birthday. Members of the faction study the works of Mao and the Soviet dictator Joseph Stalin as part of their political education. Red Star has declared its unequivocal sympathy for Hamas and praised the “good judgement” of “our socialist siblings” in Palestine for working with the Islamist organization and “external groups like Iran, Hezbollah, and Ansarallah under a principle they call unity of the fields .” In other words, Red Star is an admirer of Iran’s notorious “Axis of Resistance.” That Romer wouldn’t critique authoritarianism in Cuba is not a lapse but an expression of her faction’s politics. Red Star’s stated policy couldn’t be any clearer about this: “To publicly critique a government or movement that stands in opposition to the American government is to do the U.S. State Department’s work for them, from Iran to Palestine.” In other words, any state or group that opposes the American government should be beyond criticism. Liberation, the DSA’s “Marxist-Leninist-Maoist caucus,” likewise declares the United States to be “not a nation” but a “prison-house of nations, with the Euro-Americans being the jailer.” Unlike Romer, Siddique belongs to the mainstream wing of the DSA, but he is bound by the group’s statements and broader culture. The sectarian wing currently dominates the DSA: The group’s convention in Chicago last year rejected a resolution opposing “all governments that engage in the repression of democratic rights.” Thus, when asked repeatedly what he thought of Fidel Castro, whom the DSA had praised in an earlier statement, Siddique awkwardly referred to “inequality in the United States” and criticized U.S. policy—deflecting the question and offering sound bites instead of engagement, much as an establishment pol might do. [ David Brooks: Democrats became great by fighting the left ] This pro-left-authoritarian orientation explains why DSA electoral observers shamefully reported no fraud when they were dispatched to monitor the electoral sham organized by Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro in 2024. Those results were so bogus that even the left-wing governments of Brazil, Chile, and Uruguay couldn’t accept them. Yet at a DSA session on the subject, a pro-Maduro organization’s assessment that Venezuela’s electoral system was “one of the very best in the world” was presented as fact, as was the false claim that Venezuela’s main opposition candidates were “fascist.” The two wings of the DSA are committed to wildly different methods. Mamdani governs New York City partly as a technocrat, and AOC has sought to influence the Democratic Party from within. One of the DSA’s sectarian factions, by contrast, recently suggested that socialist lawmakers “should do everything in their power to disrupt any Congressional business that does not benefit the working class or advance the socialist program.” They should, it went on, “creatively abuse their powers to make it difficult to conduct legislative business,” for instance by packing the galleries of Congress with hecklers. This faction seems to view elected lawmakers as “tribunes” for the socialist movement rather than as people who, you know, make laws. The sectarian wing got the DSA to drop its endorsement of AOC and refuse to support Kamala Harris in the 2024 presidential election. Red Star argued against endorsing AOC unless she withdrew her support for Joe Biden (then the Democratic nominee), and it refused to fundraise for the Democratic leadership or central congressional campaign. But ultimately, the DSA dropped AOC on the grounds that she was not sufficiently anti-Israel—a singular obsession of the sectarian wing. (The foreign-policy section of the DSA’s political platform discusses the details of only one country’s politics, and that’s Israel and Palestine, in which it calls for the self-determination of Palestinians without making a similar provision for Israeli Jews.) For all of the extremist wing’s influence, however, my years of research into the group suggest that the DSA’s members are mostly not members of any caucuses. The average DSA member probably has more in common with AOC than with Mao or Hamas, and the nonsectarians seem especially dominant in the group’s large urban chapters—such as in New York City, where the DSA has more than 15,000 of its approximately 120,000 members . More than 80 percent of DSA members in the Bronx and Queens voted in 2024 to endorse AOC. The sectarian wing came to control much of the organization’s leadership by manipulating internal processes, which is one reason it opposes organizational referenda and other one-member-one-vote procedures. The DSA’s mainstream wing includes thinkers who are committed to democracy, critical of authoritarianism (including that of socialist regimes, past and present), and who reject some of the signature policies of the sectarian wing, such as police abolition. These figures have been vocal in response to last month’s media fiasco. Eric Blanc, a labor historian at Rutgers, sharply criticized Romer for “falling into a trap being set by the establishment,” which seeks “to paint DSA as extreme.” Like others in his wing, Blanc advocates for adopting a Nordic-style social democracy as a step toward overcoming capitalism. This position is also shared by the Jacobin founder and former DSA Vice Chair Bhaskar Sunkara, whose 2019 Socialist Manifesto explores Swedish social democracy in envisioning a socialism for the 21st century. [ James Kirchick: The DSA is a parasite ] Reacting to the DSA’s recent media debacles, Ben Burgis, a philosopher and Jacobin writer, opined : “We don’t do ourselves any favors by refusing to say anything too negative about left-wing dictatorships targeted by US foreign policy,” especially “if we’re trying to argue that the failures of authoritarian state socialism in the twentieth century shouldn’t mean that capitalism is the best humanity will ever be able to do.” The group has failed to reassure its critics of its commitment to multiparty democracy, Burgis added. Thinkers in this wing of the DSA take seriously the imperative to reconcile socialist commitments to economic justice with democratic and liberal values. Burgis, Sunkara, and the economist Mike Beggs have co-authored a forthcoming book called The Blueprint: How Socialism Can Work in the Real World , which attempts to offer a “realistic model” of a post-capitalist economic system. Drawing on the work of the liberal philosopher John Rawls, as well as detailed economic research, the book takes the Soviet Union to task for a “record of systematic economic failure, not just political repression” and suggests a model that mixes social ownership with a significant role for the market. It also engages the arguments of well-known critics of socialism, such as Friedrich Hayek and Ludwig von Mises. This work puts the flippancy of Romer’s “taxing the hell out of millionaires” comment to shame. But if the likes of AOC, Sunkara, Burgis, and Blanc wish for the American public to give their notions of an economically rigorous and democratically committed socialism a chance, they need to break with the fans of Mao and Hamas. So long as they share an organization with the DSA’s sectarians, they can’t complain when the media associates the DSA—and American socialism—with the extreme positions that it formally adopts and that its leaders espouse. No amount of media training can solve that.

items.title: The Charges Were Dropped, but the Damage Was Already Done
items.description: D avid Huerta sat on a steel bed too small for his burly frame in a Los Angeles jail last summer and looked out a small rectangular window at Dodger Stadium, where he’d once spent evenings with his two boys. He was the kid who’d made good, although it hadn’t been easy. His mother died from breast cancer when he was 4. He was raised in southeast L.A. by his dad, a veteran of the Korean War turned Teamster, who paid the bills by loading and unloading cargo—and, when he was out of work, took his sons with him to the hiring hall. Huerta steered clear of gangs and instead went to college, became a union organizer, and worked his way up to become president of the largest labor union in the state, the Service Employees International Union of California. Yet here he was. He was sure that he hadn’t done anything illegal. He had screamed at masked federal agents as they executed search warrants at a downtown apparel business that was suspected of hiring undocumented immigrants. He had been angry, no question—especially at President Trump. He had flipped his middle fingers at the masked federal officers. At one point, he sat down in front of the business’s gate; later, he encouraged other protesters to form a picket circle in front of it. When an officer warned him he might be arrested, he replied, “I can’t hear you through your fucking mask.” And when a police van tried to enter, he stood with his hands on his hips nearby. He considered all of that well within the bounds of his First Amendment rights. But he couldn’t stop second-guessing his decision to show up at such a volatile scene alone. Huerta wondered how his wife and sons, his niece and nephew, and his other family members would react to seeing videos of his arrest. He wondered if he had somehow jeopardized the safety of his union’s hundreds of thousands of members by drawing unwanted headlines. He wondered if his arrest would make others more fearful of opposing this administration’s actions. He wondered when he would be released—or if he would be. He wondered if he could survive prison, should it come to that. And he wondered what his late dad would’ve thought of him sitting on a thin, stained mattress as his cellmate on the top bunk managed a comedown from drugs. Would he have been ashamed, or proud? Trump’s top federal prosecutor in Los Angeles charged Huerta with conspiracy to impede a federal officer—a felony, under a Civil War–era statute that had rarely been used before last year. If convicted, Huerta faced up to six years in prison. But months later, prosecutors lessened the charges to a misdemeanor count of obstructing, resisting, or opposing a federal officer. This July, the Justice Department said it would drop the charges altogether, adding it to the growing list of federal prosecutions that have fallen apart before going to trial. Although those dismissals have been celebrated as victories, the cases have taken a financial and psychological toll on the defendants. For Huerta, the past 15 months have been filled with anxiety. He has endured sleepless nights and grown emotionally distant from his wife of 30 years. The public attention continues to make it more difficult to do his job. And despite his pride in standing for what he believed in, he struggles with the shame of being jailed and appearing in court in shackles—an image he worries that his two sons and niece and nephew (whom he has raised as his own) will never forget. As we spoke inside a coffee shop in his neighborhood of Highland Park one recent afternoon, Huerta’s voice rose in anger and indignation while he recounted and, at times, reenacted the minutes before he was shoved to the ground by a federal officer. He teared up. “The president of the union just got fucking arrested,” he said. “If they can do this to me, imagine what they’re doing to other people.” O n the morning of June 6, 2025, the phones at the SEIU office were ringing with reported sightings of immigration-enforcement operations in and around downtown L.A. Huerta and his team—along with other labor leaders, Democrats, and social-justice groups—had been preparing for a moment like this ever since Trump was elected to a second term. The administration was trying to detain and deport as many immigrants as possible. Workplaces were being targeted, and even American-born Latinos were getting caught up in immigration dragnets. Huerta and his team would later learn that this day was the opening of a monthslong operation in the L.A. area overseen by then–Border Patrol Commander Gregory Bovino. It aimed to not just increase arrest numbers but also intimidate immigrant communities. [ Read: A U.S. citizen detained by ICE for three days tells his story ] The union’s rapid-response network was designed to help employees during moments like this. “Shit’s happening,” Huerta recalled thinking that morning, “and we’re now in the fight.” He heard a report of an immigration raid in the apparel district, so he scrapped his plans and headed there. Federal agents were swarming an industrial complex. A woman stood outside the facility’s gate, prosecutors later claimed in charging documents, filming officers and telling someone by phone what was happening. A federal agent later said that Huerta seemed to be communicating with that woman and other protesters “in a concerted effort to disrupt” the operation. As the crowd grew, people screamed expletives at the officers, and someone yelled, “I want you to kill yourself,” according to the accounts of federal agents contained in court filings. The agents described Huerta joining in the taunting, urging protesters to “walk in circles and picket,” and pacing in front of the gate, “effectively preventing law enforcement vehicles from entering or exiting.” Huerta told me that he had never acted quite like this at a protest, but that he had snapped when he saw how the officers were treating a young girl who was crying about her dad, who she said was inside the building. “They were so dismissive of her,” he said. He screamed at the agents, asking how targeting workers was making the city safer, and telling them that they were “taking orders from a fucking monster.” When a federal agent ordered Huerta to move away from the gate, he remained in place, confident that the vehicles had plenty of room. An officer then began to move Huerta out of the way. He recalls not fighting back and keeping his hands on his hips—just as he was trained. But he was still pushed to the ground. A video shows Huerta falling on his back, his head hitting the curb. He told me that he was rolled onto his stomach, sprayed with a chemical irritant, cuffed, and taken to the hospital, where he spent several hours before being transferred to a federal detention center. His wife, Lucía Aguayo-Huerta, learned of his arrest while at the doctor. His oldest son, Ismael, heard from a cousin, who was crying hysterically. He jumped on Instagram and typed in his father’s name. Huerta had a bum shoulder from an old skiing injury. His other son, Camilo, watched as Huerta’s arm was pulled behind his back in one of the videos. “I was almost on the verge of tears,” he told me. “Almost screaming at my phone, like, You’re fucking with his shoulder! ” Huerta didn’t sleep that first night in jail, and when he arrived at breakfast, he squirreled away packaged food in case it would become valuable in the days ahead. He’d been fingerprinted for detention on a Friday night but had not been fully processed and so had no way to call his family, although he’d briefly called his wife, Lucía, while he was at the hospital. Protests had erupted in parts of downtown Los Angeles as word of the raids spread. Outside the detention facility, people were showing up in large numbers, clashing at times with police. Inside, news of those protests streamed on a TV. At one point, an inmate looked back and forth from the TV to Huerta, and asked Huerta if that was him on-screen. “That’s me, bro,” Huerta replied. He said the man asked, You’re the fucking union president? What the fuck are you doing here? His title, and years spent helping workers, made his life over the next 48 hours easier. Another inmate gave him toilet paper, a cup, and toothpaste, the holy trinity of jail provisions. Word spread, Huerta told me, and soon 100 or so men had gathered to applaud him. It was a demonstration of support that Huerta hadn’t realized he needed. The sense of community he felt in that moment reminded him of his own union and the solidarity shown by his dad’s old Teamster buddies, who’d rallied around their family after his mom died, bringing them money and bags of food. He spent the rest of that day learning about the other men and the circumstances that had landed them in jail, in hopes of helping them after his release. The hardest part of all, Huerta said, was when his wife and kids showed up for his arraignment and bail hearing and he had to look them in the eye. He wore a black T-shirt, black jeans, cuffs, and shackles. From his perspective, it was humiliating. From theirs, it was honorable. His sons told me that their dad had held his head high, his shoulders back, and his chest straight. Listen [ : When Border Patrol comes to town ] Dozens of other union leaders and workers packed the courtroom to support Huerta, along with Democratic Senator Adam Schiff. Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass wrote a letter to the judge, urging her to take into account his ties and contributions to the community as she decided bail. Huerta was charged with conspiracy, released on $50,000 bond, and dropped outside without his shoes. Facing a throng of supporters, he defended his actions and spoke of the men he had met who were still stuck inside. “We will have our time for justice,” he told the crowd, “but we must do it in a way that we demonstrate the power of working people.” That night, though, after a long shower and dinner from his favorite taco truck, Huerta lay awake in his bed thinking about a new, terrifying phrase: “conspiracy to impede.” T he psychological stress was, Huerta later realized, his worst punishment. He wanted to get back to work, but he didn’t want his presence at the office to draw negative attention to the union. For a time, he worked remotely. Lucía and the boys worried about his health. He had grown moody and snippy, often wanting to be left alone after work. Other family members worried that Huerta’s critics might try to physically harm him. Three attorneys and their teams from Los Angeles and Washington, D.C., represented him pro bono, and nonprofits helped pay other expenses. But Huerta was still stressed about the many hundreds of hours that his case was consuming. All of the time he was spending on his legal fight was time lost organizing laborers, he said. Senator Alex Padilla of California, a Democrat, told me he figured that the federal government’s case against Huerta, a friend, would fail, but he knew it had to be taken seriously. “It was clear to me that it was weighing on him,” Padilla said. But Huerta also understood, the senator said, that his members were “looking to him for how to handle the chaos that was going on and the pain that was being inflicted.” “Free David Huerta” rallies popped up around the state; supporters carried posters featuring his stenciled portrait and wore T-shirts emblazoned with his name. “An injury to one,” the AFL-CIO wrote on Facebook, “is an injury to all.” Huerta attended two rallies to protest Trump’s immigration policies, but kept his appearances short, he told me. He left one as people marched toward a detention facility; he didn’t want to violate the terms of his bond that required he stay at least 100 yards away from federal-law-enforcement agents or operations. One day, while at home with Lucía, he paced the house and imagined how much worse things could get, feeling out of control. “Hey, calm down, you’re okay,” his wife told him. He later realized that he had suffered an anxiety attack. He was raised in a culture in which seeking treatment for mental health carries a stigma, but he knew he needed help. He began to see a therapist for the first time. In October, his charge was downgraded to a misdemeanor. Prosecutors needed to establish that he had planned to interfere with federal officers that day—but his actions were unplanned, his attorneys said. His team tried to get prosecutors to dismiss the case entirely. The lesser charges brought some relief, but his character and reputation were still under attack. “Those anxieties of uncertainty,” he said, “they kept creeping up.” The case continued to weigh heavily on his marriage. Then, in July, prosecutors gave up. Late last month, the charge was dismissed with prejudice. He got back his passport and phone, two items that symbolize his freedom and his work. He did not celebrate. “I was detained—and fortunately, that’s all that happened,” he told me. Others—in Minneapolis, Houston, Maine—had been shot dead while interacting with immigration officers. Bill Essayli, the top federal prosecutor in Los Angeles, said on X that Huerta, since his arrest, had complied with conditions to not interfere with federal agents and operations, but “should he unlawfully interfere with any federal agent engaged in their duties, we will not hesitate to arrest and charge him again.” His office declined further comment. [ Read: Another fatal ICE shooting ] If the point was to try to make an example out of him, a conviction wasn’t necessary. The case against Huerta signaled to the labor and immigrant communities that no one could protest immigration raids without real risk, he and other labor leaders told me. Some union members grew afraid of speaking out, they said. But many others were moved to show their disapproval of the immigration crackdown by protesting peacefully because of how they saw officers treat Huerta, Arnulfo De La Cruz, who took over in April as president of SEIU California, told me. “In a lot of ways, he was the embodiment of a transition from fear to We’re not gonna back down .” Huerta doesn’t know when—or even if—he will show up at another immigration-enforcement protest, he said. His experience has made him think hard about how he tries to achieve his goals. “I’m not leaving the work,” he told me. “But I would be a liar to say that it’s not in the back of my head that I could find myself in the same situation.” On the day I saw him, he had just pulled into town from Big Bear, a rare escape. He spoke not of the views or the lake, but of the workers powering the restaurants and hotels.

items.title: El odio de los conductores al carril bus-VAO “vacío” frena su expansión: “No hay que mirar cuántos vehículos pasan sino a cuánta gente llevan”
items.description: La DGT y el Ministerio de Transportes han probado durante un mes un nuevo modelo de carril bus-VAO (vehículos de alta ocupación) en la A2 a su entrada en Madrid. El ensayo, que ha tardado 10 años en realizarse, dedica a autobuses y coches compartidos el carril izquierdo de la vía solo en hora punta, y es mucho más barato que los modelos que requieren grandes obras, como el de la A6. Transportes —entonces Fomento— planeó construir este tipo de vías en todas las entradas a Madrid, pero el plan se quedó en un cajón por la crisis de 2008. Los expertos consideran que el sesgo de los conductores ante el “carril vacío” y la falta de coordinación entre Administraciones frenan la implantación de estas infraestructuras, que mejoran la eficiencia del transporte público y son necesarias en todas las ciudades. Por ahora solo hay unos cuantos ejemplos en toda España. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Sécurité des bâtiments : les maires et les ordres professionnels scellent un partenariat
items.description: © DR Face à la recrudescence des effondrements d'immeubles, les Communes et Villes Unies du Cameroun (CVUC), l'Ordre National des Architectes du Cameroun (ONAC) et l'Ordre National des Ingénieurs de Génie Civil (ONIGC) ont signé ce mercredi 03 septembre 2026 une convention-cadre tripartite historique. Objectif : verrouiller le suivi des chantiers privés après la délivrance du permis de construire. C'est une réponse directe à une crise qui endeuille le Cameroun. Les CVUC, l'ONAC et l'ONIGC ont décidé de siffler la fin du désordre dans le secteur du BTP. Réunies le 03 septembre, les trois parties ont paraphé une convention qui change la donne. Fini le permis de construire délivré puis oublié. Désormais, le dispositif impose une maîtrise d'œuvre conjointe associant obligatoirement architecte et ingénieur sur les chantiers privés. Le texte prévoit des garde-fous concrets : instauration d'un carnet de suivi de chantier, obligation de points d'arrêt aux étapes critiques des travaux pour validation, et mécanisme de paiement progressif des honoraires des professionnels pour éviter les abandons. L'ambition politique est claire : prévenir les malfaçons, stopper les modifications anarchiques des plans approuvés et surtout, redonner aux mairies leur pouvoir de contrôle administratif, souvent contourné. Pour ne pas brusquer le système, une phase pilote sera lancée dans des communes volontaires, avec deux innovations majeures : la digitalisation du carnet de suivi et la formation des agents municipaux. À travers cet accord, les collectivités et les ordres professionnels envoient un message fort : la sécurité des populations prime sur les économies de bout de chandelle. Cet article Sécurité des bâtiments : les maires et les ordres professionnels scellent un partenariat est apparu en premier sur Journalducameroun.com .

items.title: Cameroun/ Fiscalité : mise en demeure des hautes personnalités et fonctionnaires
items.description: © DR Dans un communiqué signé le 02 septembre 2026, le Ministre des Finances annonce la fin du délai de déclaration de l'IRPP et de la TPF pour l'exercice 2025. Les retardataires, notamment les hautes personnalités et les salariés du public et parapublic, ont sept jours pour se régulariser sous peine de sanctions lourdes, dont la publication de leurs noms dans la presse. Le ton se durcit à la Direction Générale des Impôts. Dans un communiqué signé le 02 septembre 2026, le Ministre Louis Paul Motaze rappelle que les délais de souscription de la déclaration annuelle de l'Impôt sur le Revenu des Personnes Physiques (IRPP) et de la Taxe sur la Propriété Foncière (TPF) sont arrivés à échéance. Initialement fixés au 31 juillet 2026 puis prorogés au 30 août 2026, ces délais concernaient spécifiquement les contribuables non professionnels de la catégorie des hautes personnalités et les salariés des secteurs public et parapublic. Si le Ministre félicite ceux qui se sont acquittés de leurs obligations, il lance un ultimatum aux retardataires. À compter de la publication du communiqué, qui vaut mise en demeure, ils disposent d'un délai de sept jours pour régulariser leur situation conformément à l'article L 3 du Livre des Procédures Fiscales. Passé ce délai, l'administration fiscale promet une tolérance zéro. Elle brandit la taxation d'office avec majorations, une amende forfaitaire de 100 000 FCFA prévue à l'article L 99, et surtout, l'arme politique : la publication de la liste des défaillants par voie de presse en application de l'article L3 bis du Code Général des Impôts. Une mesure de "name and shame" qui vise directement l'élite administrative camerounaise. Cet article Cameroun/ Fiscalité : mise en demeure des hautes personnalités et fonctionnaires est apparu en premier sur Journalducameroun.com .

items.title: Alibandeng : privés d’eau, des habitants interpellent Oligui Nguema
items.description: À l’heure où les élèves reprenaient le chemin de l’école ce lundi 7 septembre, quelques habitants d’Alibandeng, dans le premier arrondissement de Libreville, ont choisi de battre le pavé pour dénoncer leurs difficultés d’accès à l’eau potable. Pancartes en main et bonbonnes vides aux pieds, ils appellent les autorités, notamment le chef de l’État, à mettre fin à une situation qui, selon eux, dure depuis plusieurs mois, voire plusieurs années. Des habitantes d'Alibandeng manifestant leur colère, le 7 septembre 2026. © GabonReview À Alibandeng, la rentrée scolaire n’a pas commencé dans la sérénité pour tout le monde. Dès 8 heures, une poignée de riverains s’est retrouvée au lieu-dit Carrefour la Pompe pour faire entendre son ras-le-bol. Dans une atmosphère à la fois tendue et résignée, les manifestants brandissent des pancartes et répètent inlassablement le même mot d’ordre : «On veut de l’eau !» Le décor en dit long sur leur exaspération. Des bonbonnes vides posées au sol, des pancartes improvisées et des habitants venus témoigner d’un quotidien rythmé par l’attente du précieux liquide. Pour certains, l’eau ne coule au robinet qu’un ou deux jours par semaine. Pour d’autres, elle a tout simplement disparu depuis des mois, voire des années, selon les secteurs. «On veut de l’eau ! Alibandeng veut de l’eau !» «On veut de l’eau ! Alibandeng veut de l’eau ! L’eau, c’est la vie. Trop, c’est trop !» , lance Brice*, pancarte à la main. Le choix du jour n’est pas anodin. «C’est la rentrée scolaire, nous avons besoin d’eau. Nous sommes dans la 5e République. Il n’est plus concevable d’être privé du minimum qu’est l’eau potable» , poursuit-il, avant d’interpeller directement le président de la République. «Monsieur le président de la République, Son Excellence Brice Clotaire Oligui Nguema, intervenez. Faites quelque chose, s’il vous plaît. Vous êtes le père de la Nation» , implore-t-il. Sur l’une des faces de sa pancarte, le message est sans ambiguïté : «On veut de l’eau à Alibandeng dans toutes les maisons.» Sur l’autre, une formule plus ironique : «Non à la poussée d’Archimède.» Une manière pour ce riverain de tourner en dérision l’une des explications techniques avancées, selon les habitants, au président de la République pour justifier les disparités d’approvisionnement en eau observées dans certaines zones du Grand Libreville. Des réserves pour survivre au quotidien © GabonReview Dans les foyers concernés, l’irrégularité de la distribution impose une organisation quasi permanente. Lorsque l’eau revient, il faut remplir les récipients disponibles afin de constituer des réserves pour les jours suivants. Une pratique qui n’est pas sans risques sanitaires, mais à laquelle certains habitants disent être contraints faute d’alternative. Assise à même le bitume, Jeanne*, une pancarte posée devant elle et plusieurs bonbonnes vides à ses côtés, laisse éclater sa colère. «Nous ne voulons plus l’eau des puits ou celle des forages, qui nous rendent malades ; et nous n’avons pas d’argent pour nous faire livrer de l’eau» , lâche-t-elle. Derrière la revendication collective se dessinent ainsi des difficultés très concrètes : se laver, cuisiner, nettoyer, assurer l’hygiène des enfants ou encore préparer leur rentrée scolaire deviennent des exercices quotidiens. «Les locataires quittent nos maisons» La pénurie aurait également des conséquences sur le logement dans le quartier. «Les locataires quittent nos maisons parce qu’il n’y a pas d’eau dans les robinets. Nos maisons sont vides depuis des mois» , affirme Annette*, visiblement préoccupée. À quelques jours de la rentrée, son inquiétude porte surtout sur les enfants : «C’est la rentrée. Comment ferons-nous pour envoyer nos enfants à l’école cette année ?» Une question qui traduit, au-delà du problème d’approvisionnement, le sentiment d’abandon exprimé par ces habitants. De l’eau potable… qui coule dans la rue © GabonReview La mobilisation prend une dimension particulièrement symbolique lorsque des riverains conduisent Gabonreview à quelques centaines de mètres du lieu du rassemblement, au lieu-dit «derrière le Grand Collège». Là, au beau milieu de la chaussée, de l’eau s’échappe d’une plaque d’égout et s’écoule continuellement sur la route. Pour les habitants, le contraste est difficile à accepter : alors qu’ils remplissent des bidons lorsque l’eau revient aux robinets, une importante quantité d’eau potable semble se perdre dans la rue. «Ça fait plusieurs mois que ça dure, mais la SEEG ne semble pas pressée d’intervenir. C’est pourtant de l’eau qui aurait pu servir aux populations de ce quartier» , peste un riverain. Sur place, tout laisse penser qu’une conduite située sous la plaque d’égout présente une défaillance. Une fuite dont l’ampleur et la nature devront toutefois être établies par les services compétents. Reste que, pour les habitants d’Alibandeng, l’image est devenue difficilement supportable : d’un côté, des robinets à sec ; de l’autre, de l’eau qui se perd sur la chaussée. Au terme de cette matinée de protestation, leur revendication tient en quelques mots, répétés comme un leitmotiv : de l’eau, régulièrement et dans toutes les maisons. À quand une intervention de la Société d’énergie et d’eau du Gabon (SEEG) sur cette fuite ? Et surtout, à quand un approvisionnement régulier en eau potable pour les habitants d’Alibandeng ? *Prénoms modifiés à la demande des intéressés. L’article Alibandeng : privés d’eau, des habitants interpellent Oligui Nguema est apparu en premier sur Gabonreview.com | Actualité du Gabon | .

items.title: Feijóo y Vivas acusan a Marruecos de lanzar un ataque sobre Ceuta para conseguir “algún tipo de cesión” de España
items.description: El Partido Popular en pleno ha arropado este lunes al presidente de Ceuta, Juan Jesús Vivas, que se ha presentado en Madrid para dar la voz de alarma sobre la situación de la ciudad autónoma un mes después de la entrada masiva de unos 70.000 inmigrantes. “Ceuta es una olla a presión que en cualquier momento puede estallar”, ha alertado Vivas en un desayuno informativo en la capital al que ha asistido toda la cúpula nacional del PP, cargos europeos, exministros y hasta siete presidentes autonómicos populares. El líder del PP, Alberto Núñez Feijóo, y el mandatario ceutí han acusado a Marruecos de haber intentado una maniobra con la “invasión” de Ceuta, que según el líder del PP estaba destinada a arrancar a España concesiones. “Estoy seguro de que la reacción del presidente Vivas y de todo su pueblo, seguida posteriormente por la mayoría de los españoles, ha frustrado un plan que empezaba por una invasión, que seguía con la resignación y terminaba con algún tipo de cesión al país vecino”, ha afirmado Feijóo. El presidente ceutí se ha opuesto al traslado de los inmigrantes a la Península para descongestionar a la ciudad, incluidos los menores, con el respaldo de todo el PP. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Adidas ciblée par une campagne de boycott à cause d’Israël
items.description: Adidas, l’équipementier de l’équipe d’Algérie de football, rejoint la longue liste de firmes occidentales ciblées par une campagne de boycott pour leur soutien à Israël. Il est reproché à l’équipementier sportif allemand d'avoir mis en exergue un soldat israélien dans une publicité. Alors que des milliers de Palestiniens ont été estropiés dans la bande de Gaza du fait de l’agression israélienne, la marque aux trois bandes a choisi l'image d'un soldat israélien amputé pour lancer un nouveau service. Pour les défenseurs de la cause palestinienne, c’est un parti pris flagrant et un mépris pour les milliers de victimes palestiniennes. Ce n’est pas la première fois qu’Adidas se retrouve dans une telle polémique. Adidas met en avant un soldat israélien amputé : un mépris pour les milliers d'estropiés palestiniens Le nouveau service, « Single shoe service », est a priori louable. Il s’agit de donner la possibilité aux personnes qui ont perdu un pied d'acheter seulement la chaussure dont elles ont besoin au lieu d’une paire. Sauf que la manière dont la campagne de communication a été lancée est très contestable. Adidas is facing calls for a boycott after featuring a former Israeli soldier in a campaign promoting its single-shoe service for amputees. Shalev Biton lost a leg in Gaza, with a social media campaign emphasising more than 5,000 Palestinians also lost limbs. pic.twitter.com/hbOFzmwxZI — Al Jazeera English (@AJEnglish) September 7, 2026 Les communicants d’Adidas ont choisi le soldat israélien Shalev Biton qui a perdu une jambe près de la bande de Gaza en 2021. Or, l'agression israélienne contre cette même enclave palestinienne, déclenchée en octobre 2023, a fait des milliers d’estropiés. Le territoire abrite aujourd'hui la plus forte concentration d’amputés au monde. Selon les statistiques officielles de l’OMS, l’agression israélienne a causé 5 000 amputations traumatiques et plus de 22 000 blessures graves aux membres. Save the Children et l’UNICEF avaient indiqué en janvier 2024 qu’au moins 10 enfants de Gaza avaient perdu une jambe ou les deux chaque jour depuis octobre 2023. Mettre en exergue dans un tel contexte un soldat israélien est incompréhensible. Pour le politologue français Pascal Boniface, “c’est une bourde au mieux, et si ce n'est pas une bourde, c’est encore pire”. Des appels au boycott des produits Adidas Des appels au boycott ont aussitôt été lancés. Javier Bardem, l'acteur espagnol connu pour son soutien à la cause palestinienne, a appelé ses abonnés à boycotter les produits de la marque allemande. De nombreux internautes et organisations soutenant la Palestine ont lancé des appels similaires tant en Occident que dans des pays musulmans. Pour le commentateur politique britannique Sami Hamdi, Adidas pourrait subir des conséquences similaires à celles rencontrées par d’autres grandes marques boycottées pour les mêmes raisons, comme McDonald’s, Starbucks et KFC qui ont été contraintes de fermer des succursales dans plusieurs pays musulmans. Face à la polémique, la marque a réagi. “Nous sommes conscients que certaines interprétations diffusées ces derniers jours ont présenté de manière erronée l’objectif de ce service”, a écrit l’entreprise. En 2024, Adidas s’est retrouvé au centre de critiques après avoir cédé à la pression d’Israël et annulé la participation à une campagne publicitaire du mannequin Bella Hadid, pro-palestinienne . L’article Adidas ciblée par une campagne de boycott à cause d'Israël est apparu en premier sur TSA .

items.title: RSF releases four journalists and lawyer after months in detention in North Darfur
items.description: The Rapid Support Forces (RSF) have released four female journalists and a lawyer in Nyala, the capital of South Darfur, after holding them for varying periods of time. Sources tell Radio Dabanga that the journalists, Dr Manahil Mustafa, Ishraqa Abdelrahman, Mawahib Ibrahim, and Zahra Mohamed El Hassan, were released alongside the lawyer, Magda Hassan Ali, after about six months in detention. The journalists and lawyer were arrested after taking part in a workshop held in February that discussed women’s issues and rights. Meanwhile, the family of El Hadi Abdelrahman, the former director general of the Ministry of Education, tells Radio Dabanga that the Rapid Support Forces have also released him after he spent more than a year and a half in Dagris prison in South Darfur. This report follows coverage by Radio Dabanga last week that the Sudanese Journalists’ Syndicate says five of its members remain victims of enforced disappearance, with their fate and whereabouts still unknown. It describes this as a serious violation of their basic rights, international law, and their right to life and personal safety. In a statement, the syndicate calls for the immediate disclosure of the journalists’ fate and whereabouts, and for a serious, independent investigation into the circumstances of their disappearance. Note: This report has been translated from Arabic with the assistance of artificial intelligence tools, and subsequently reviewed and adapted by a human editor before publication. items.title: Universités publiques : Le Ministère de l’Enseignement supérieur promet la fin totale des retards académiques d’ici le 21 septembre 2026
items.description: Le ministre de l’Enseignement supérieur, de la Recherche et de l’Innovation (MESRI), le Pr Ardjima Thiombiano, a tenu une conférence de presse, ce lundi 7 septembre 2026. L’objet de cette rencontre était de faire le point sur la résorption des retards et des chevauchements d’années académiques dans les Universités publiques du Burkina Faso. Entre janvier 2024 et août 2026, les efforts du Ministère ont permis de porter le taux de filières normalisées de 81,31 % à 99,69 %. L’objectif affiché est désormais d’atteindre 100 % d’ici au 21 septembre prochain. Les années académiques à rallonge seront bientôt conjuguées au passé dans l’Énseignement supérieur public burkinabè. En moins de trois ans, le taux de filières ayant retrouvé un rythme normal est passé de 81,31 % à 99,69 %. Une performance que le Ministre de l’Enseignement supérieur, de la Recherche et de l’Innovation (MESRI), entend parachever dans les prochains jours. Selon le MESRI, en 2023, la situation était pourtant alarmante. Certaines filières accusaient des retards allant de trois à plus de trente mois, allongeant considérablement la durée des cursus. Une licence, conçue pour être obtenue en trois ans, pouvait ainsi s’étirer sur cinq années, voire davantage. Face à ce constat, le Pr Ardjima Thiombiano a expliqué que son Ministère a misé sur trois leviers complémentaires : des réformes institutionnelles, un renforcement du suivi des cursus universitaires, et la création de commissions spécialement chargées de veiller à la normalisation des filières. Cette stratégie a rapidement porté ses fruits. Le taux de normalisation, qui s’élevait à 81,31 % au 1er janvier 2024, est passé à 86,86 % au 31 juillet 2025, puis à 92,52 % avant d’atteindre 98,44 % au 31 juillet 2026. Au 31 août 2026, ce taux s’établit à 99,69 %. Sur l’ensemble des 321 filières recensées, une seule reste encore en décalage : il s’agit de la filière Pharmacie de l’Université Joseph-Ki-Zerbo (UJKZ). Sa complète régularisation est attendue pour le 21 septembre 2026. Pour le ministre Pr Thiombiano, cette avancée est inédite depuis plus de quinze ans et constitue une étape décisive dans l’assainissement du calendrier universitaire national. Lire aussi : Résorption des retards académiques dans les universités publiques : 92,52% des filières normalisées Minute.bf
